name: SatisfiesEq
doc: A point satisfies an equality constraint when the linear form vanishes there.
stmt: def SatisfiesEq (c : LinearForm R n) (x : Point R n) : Prop

name: SatisfiesLe
doc: A point satisfies a `≤` constraint when the linear form is non-positive there.
stmt: def SatisfiesLe (c : LinearForm R n) (x : Point R n) : Prop

name: SatisfiesLt
doc: A point satisfies a `<` constraint when the linear form is negative there.
stmt: def SatisfiesLt (c : LinearForm R n) (x : Point R n) : Prop

name: Satisfies
doc: Satisfaction for the unified constraint syntax.
stmt: def Satisfies (c : Constraint R n) (x : Point R n) : Prop
proof:
match c.rel with
  | .eq => SatisfiesEq c.form x
  | .le => SatisfiesLe c.form x
  | .lt => SatisfiesLt c.form x

name: Entails
doc:
A point satisfies a *set* of constraints when it satisfies every one of them.

This is the program-level notion the bridge theorems quantify over.
stmt: def Entails (cs : List (Constraint R n)) (x : Point R n) : Prop

name: Models
doc:
`H` models `c`: every point meeting every constraint in `H` also meets `c`.

This is *deliberately* stronger than `Entails`, and it is the correct target for a
"the compiled artifact preserves the meaning of the program" claim.
stmt: def Models (H : List (Constraint R n)) (c : Constraint R n) : Prop
proof:
∀ x : Point R n, Entails H x → Satisfies c x

end Satisfaction

                             

                                                                                  

section Structural

variable {R : Type} [CommSemiring R] [LinearOrder R] {n : Nat}

name: entails_cons
doc: Entailment of a cons is entailment of the head together with entailment of the tail.
stmt:
theorem entails_cons {c : Constraint R n} {cs : List (Constraint R n)} {x : Point R n} :
    Entails (c :: cs) x ↔ Satisfies c x ∧ Entails cs x
proof:
by
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact ⟨h c (List.mem_cons_self _ _),
      fun d hd => h d (List.mem_cons_of_mem _ hd)⟩
  · rintro ⟨hc, hcs⟩ d hd
    rcases List.mem_cons.mp hd with rfl | hd'
    · exact hc
    · exact hcs d hd'

name: entails_mono
doc:
Entailment is monotone in the constraint set: a superset entails at least as much.

This is the statement that a *larger* symbolic program is *stronger*, which the
embedding direction of the bridge relies on.
stmt:
theorem entails_mono {cs ds : List (Constraint R n)} {x : Point R n}
    (hsub : ∀ c ∈ cs, c ∈ ds) (h : Entails ds x) : Entails cs x
proof: fun c hc => h c (hsub c hc)

name: models_of_mem
doc: A single constraint is entailed by any set containing it.
stmt:
theorem models_of_mem {H : List (Constraint R n)} {c : Constraint R n}
    (hmem : c ∈ H) : Models H c

name: models_of_subset
doc:
Models is monotone (contravariantly) in the hypothesis set.

`models_of_subset` reads: if `H ⊆ K` (every hypothesis of `H` is also one of `K`),
then anything modelled by `H` is modelled by `K`. A point satisfying the larger set
`K` certainly satisfies the smaller one `H`.
stmt:
theorem models_of_subset {H K : List (Constraint R n)} {c : Constraint R n}
    (hsub : ∀ d ∈ H, d ∈ K) (h : Models H c) : Models K c
proof:
fun x hx => h x (entails_mono (cs := H) (ds := K) hsub hx)

end Structural

end Lattice.Core

name: AffineLayer
doc: An affine layer over a fixed width: weights and a bias on `n → ℝ`.
stmt:
structure AffineLayer (n : Type) where
                       
  W : n → n → ℝ
                     
  b : n → ℝ

name: affineAct
doc: The action of one affine layer.
stmt: noncomputable def affineAct {n : Type} [Fintype n] (p : AffineLayer n) (x : n → ℝ) : n → ℝ
proof: fun j => (∑ i, p.W i j * x i) + p.b j

name: netAct
doc:
A stack of same-width affine layers, applied left to right.

Defined by `List.foldl` so that the empty stack is the identity and appending stacks composes them
in order -- the two facts `netAct_nil` and `netAct_append` record.
stmt:
noncomputable def netAct {n : Type} [Fintype n] (ls : List (AffineLayer n)) (x : n → ℝ) :
    n → ℝ
proof: ls.foldl (fun acc p => affineAct p acc) x

name: netAct_nil
doc: The empty stack is the identity.
stmt:
@[simp] theorem netAct_nil {n : Type} [Fintype n] (x : n → ℝ) :
    netAct ([] : List (AffineLayer n)) x = x

name: netAct_append
doc:
**Composition law.** A stack of two stacks is the second applied to the first.

This is what lets a multi-layer network be reasoned about as a single map, and it is the form the
ladder needs if a stack is to be treated as one rung.
stmt:
theorem netAct_append {n : Type} [Fintype n] (ls ms : List (AffineLayer n)) (x : n → ℝ) :
    netAct (ls ++ ms) x = netAct ms (netAct ls x)

name: relu
doc: The rectifier, as a function on the reals.
stmt: def relu (x : ℝ) : ℝ

name: relu_not_injective
doc: `relu` is not injective: both `-1` and `0` map to `0`.
stmt: theorem relu_not_injective : ¬ Function.Injective relu
proof:
by
  intro h
  have hz : relu (-1) = relu 0 := by
    simp only [relu]
    norm_num
  have : (-1 : ℝ) = 0 := h hz
  norm_num at this

name: reluVec
doc: Componentwise rectification of a vector.
stmt: noncomputable def reluVec {n : Type} (x : n → ℝ) : n → ℝ

name: netRelu_not_injective
doc:
**A stack followed by an activation is not injective.**

`n := Fin 1` suffices: the two inputs that differ only in sign are both mapped to `0` by `relu`,
regardless of the stack, so the whole map collapses them.
stmt:
theorem netRelu_not_injective :
    ¬ Function.Injective (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => reluVec (netAct [] x))
proof:
by
  intro h
                                          
  have hsame : reluVec (netAct ([] : List (AffineLayer (Fin 1))) (fun _ => (-1 : ℝ)))
      = reluVec (netAct ([] : List (AffineLayer (Fin 1))) (fun _ => (0 : ℝ))) := by
    funext j
    simp only [reluVec, netAct, List.foldl_nil, relu]
    norm_num
  have hinj := h hsame
  have : (fun _ : Fin 1 => (-1 : ℝ)) = (fun _ => (0 : ℝ)) := hinj
  have := congrFun this ⟨0, by decide⟩
  norm_num at this

name: reversibility_spectrum
doc:
**Reversibility depends on the representation and the structure.**

* `LinearForm`: not injective -- `Lattice.Lift.Extraction` exhibits two distinct coefficient vectors
  with the same zero set.
* One affine layer: injective -- `Lattice.Core.Weight.layer_act_injective`.
* A stack with a rectifier: not injective -- `netRelu_not_injective`.

The middle conjunct is what makes the spectrum non-trivial: a single affine layer *is* invertible,
so "the semantic layer is not invertible" is false as a blanket statement about weights.
stmt:
theorem reversibility_spectrum :
                                    
    (∀ {m n : Type} [Fintype m] [Fintype n] [DecidableEq m] {p q : LayerParams m n},
        BehaviourallyEquivalent p q → p = q)
                                              
    ∧ ¬ Function.Injective (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => reluVec (netAct [] x))
                                      
    ∧ ¬ Function.Injective relu
